claim: Dichloromethane became an important industrial solvent during World War II.
source: Dichloromethane became an important industrial solvent during World War II and is still the most prevalent chlorinated solvent today (www.eurochlor.org).
evidence: Supported by citation to www.eurochlor.org

claim: Dichloromethane is still the most prevalent chlorinated solvent today.
source: Dichloromethane became an important industrial solvent during World War II and is still the most prevalent chlorinated solvent today (www.eurochlor.org).
evidence: Supported by citation to www.eurochlor.org

claim: Several microbial strains have been isolated based on their ability to grow on DCM as the sole source of carbon and energy following widespread environmental contamination by DCM.
source: Following widespread environmental contamination by DCM, several microbial strains have been isolated based on their ability to grow on DCM as the sole source of carbon and energy.
evidence: Statement about historical isolation of DCM-degrading strains from contaminated environments

claim: Methylobacterium extorquens DM4 is a methylotrophic Alphaproteobacterium.
source: Most notably, Methylobacterium extorquens DM4, a methylotrophic Alphaproteobacterium, has served as a reference model to elucidate the details of bacterial growth with DCM (Gälli and Leisinger, 1985; Muller et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gälli and Leisinger, 1985 and Muller et al., 2011a

claim: M. extorquens DM4 has served as a reference model to elucidate the details of bacterial growth with DCM.
source: Most notably, Methylobacterium extorquens DM4, a methylotrophic Alphaproteobacterium, has served as a reference model to elucidate the details of bacterial growth with DCM (Gälli and Leisinger, 1985; Muller et al., 2011a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gälli and Leisinger, 1985 and Muller et al., 2011a

claim: M. extorquens DM4 expresses a dehalogenase, DcmA.
source: M. extorquens DM4 expresses a dehalogenase, DcmA, whose gene shows clear signs of horizontal transfer (Schmid-Appert et al., 1997; Vuilleumier et al., 2009) and whose product, formaldehyde, feeds directly into central methylotrophic metabolism (Chistoserdova, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmid-Appert et al., 1997 and Vuilleumier et al., 2009

claim: The dcmA gene shows clear signs of horizontal transfer.
source: M. extorquens DM4 expresses a dehalogenase, DcmA, whose gene shows clear signs of horizontal transfer (Schmid-Appert et al., 1997; Vuilleumier et al., 2009) and whose product, formaldehyde, feeds directly into central methylotrophic metabolism (Chistoserdova, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmid-Appert et al., 1997 and Vuilleumier et al., 2009

claim: The product of DcmA, formaldehyde, feeds directly into central methylotrophic metabolism.
source: M. extorquens DM4 expresses a dehalogenase, DcmA, whose gene shows clear signs of horizontal transfer (Schmid-Appert et al., 1997; Vuilleumier et al., 2009) and whose product, formaldehyde, feeds directly into central methylotrophic metabolism (Chistoserdova, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chistoserdova, 2011

claim: Past efforts to understand the genetics of growth on DCM used gene knockouts to uncover DCM-specific genes.
source: Past efforts to understand the genetics of growth on DCM used gene knockouts to uncover DCM-specific genes (Figure 1A) (Muller et al., 2011b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muller et al., 2011b

claim: dcmA transconjugants showed DCM dehalogenase activity but grew poorly on DCM.
source: These dcmA transconjugants showed DCM dehalogenase activity but grew poorly on DCM, and we previously investigated factors that might explain their limited growth (Michener et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michener et al., 2014

claim: Growing on DCM using the dcmA catabolic pathway produces formaldehyde, hydrochloric acid, and the alkylating agent S-chloromethylglutathione.
source: Growing on DCM using the dcmA catabolic pathway is very challenging for the host, as its products and intermediates include formaldehyde, hydrochloric acid, and the alkylating agent S-chloromethylglutathione (Figure 1F) (Kayser et al., 2000; Kayser and Vuilleumier, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kayser et al., 2000 and Kayser and Vuilleumier, 2001, and shown in Figure 1F

claim: DCM dehalogenase activity was generally high in transconjugant strains.
source: As DCM dehalogenase activity was generally high in transconjugant strains (Michener et al., 2014), we hypothesized that one or more of these stresses was limiting growth in the transconjugants and thus required post–transfer evolutionary refinement of the host to produce highly active DCM-degrading strains.
evidence: Supported by citation to Michener et al., 2014

claim: The dcmA gene was previously transferred into three strains of M. extorquens as well as three other species of Methylobacterium.
source: We previously transferred the DCM dehalogenase dcmA into three strains of M. extorquens as well as three other species of Methylobacterium (Michener et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michener et al., 2014

claim: Each of the transconjugants was significantly less fit than the natural isolate, M. extorquens DM4.
source: Each of the transconjugants was significantly less fit than the natural isolate, M. extorquens DM4 (hereafter referred to as 'DM4').
evidence: Direct statement about fitness comparison

claim: Replicate populations of five transconjugants were serially propagated with DCM as the sole carbon and energy source to select for increased fitness on DCM.
source: In this work, replicate populations of five of these transconjugants were serially propagated with DCM as the sole carbon and energy source to select for increased fitness on DCM.
evidence: Description of experimental evolution procedure

claim: M. extorquens AM1 was initially unable to grow on DCM alone and instead was propagated on a mixture of DCM and methanol.
source: One of these five transconjugants, M. extorquens AM1, was initially unable to grow on DCM alone and instead was propagated on a mixture of DCM and methanol.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions for AM1

claim: After a total of 150 generations of growth, individual clones were isolated from each replicate population.
source: After a total of 150 generations of growth, individual clones were isolated from each replicate population.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure

claim: For four out of the five ancestral transconjugant strains, the fitness of isolates from each evolved population was significantly higher than the fitness of the ancestor during growth on DCM.
source: For four out of the five ancestral transconjugant strains, the fitness of isolates from each evolved population was significantly higher than the fitness of the ancestor during growth on DCM (Figure 2), increasing by 1.6- to 13-fold relative to the respective ancestral transconjugant.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: The fitness of evolved isolates increased by 1.6- to 13-fold relative to the respective ancestral transconjugant.
source: For four out of the five ancestral transconjugant strains, the fitness of isolates from each evolved population was significantly higher than the fitness of the ancestor during growth on DCM (Figure 2), increasing by 1.6- to 13-fold relative to the respective ancestral transconjugant.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2

claim: Methylobacterium radiotolerans was the only transconjugant that did not yield improved isolates after 150 generations.
source: Methylobacterium radiotolerans was the only transconjugant that did not yield improved isolates after 150 generations, and these non-improved populations were not further characterized.
evidence: Direct statement about M. radiotolerans evolution results

claim: The genomes of all ancestral strains had previously been sequenced.
source: The genomes of all ancestral strains had previously been sequenced (Vuilleumier et al., 2009; Marx et al., 2012), so we used a combination of whole-genome resequencing and targeted Sanger sequencing to identify putative causal mutations in the evolved isolates.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vuilleumier et al., 2009 and Marx et al., 2012

claim: In the seven isolates that were resequenced, mutations were repeatedly found to the genes for the protein translocase secY, the chloride/proton antiporter clcA, and a hypothetical protein with a domain of unknown function (DUF599, renamed edgA), as well as a single mutation to besA.
source: In the seven isolates that we resequenced, we repeatedly found mutations to the genes for the protein translocase secY, the chloride/proton antiporter clcA, and a hypothetical protein with a domain of unknown function (DUF599, which we renamed edgA for Evolved Dichloromethane Growth), as well as a single mutation to besA, a homolog of the eukaryal bestrophin family of chloride channels (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by whole-genome resequencing data shown in Figure 3A

claim: BesA is a homolog of the eukaryal bestrophin family of chloride channels.
source: In the seven isolates that we resequenced, we repeatedly found mutations to the genes for the protein translocase secY, the chloride/proton antiporter clcA, and a hypothetical protein with a domain of unknown function (DUF599, which we renamed edgA for Evolved Dichloromethane Growth), as well as a single mutation to besA, a homolog of the eukaryal bestrophin family of chloride channels (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct statement about BesA homology

claim: Each individual mutation to secY, clcA, besA, and edgA was beneficial when reconstructed in AM1 and PA1.
source: We then measured the fitness of the reconstructed mutants against the natural isolate, DM4. Each of the mutations was highly beneficial, regardless of whether the mutation arose in that host during evolution (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by competitive fitness data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The mutations had only minor fitness effects during growth on succinate, indicating that their beneficial effects were specific to the challenge of growing on DCM.
source: In contrast, the mutations had only minor fitness effects during growth on an alternate carbon source, succinate, indicating that their beneficial effects were specific to the challenge of growing on DCM and were not broadly beneficial during laboratory growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The fitness effects of single mutations were not additive.
source: While each of the single mutations was beneficial, the fitness effects were not additive.
evidence: Supported by double mutant fitness data

claim: In isolate E2, the besAE2/clcAE2 double mutant has similar fitness to the besAE2 single mutant when grown on DCM.
source: For example, isolate E2 contained mutations in both clcA and besA. Each of these mutations was beneficial alone, but the double mutant was no more fit than the besAE2 single mutant (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by competitive fitness data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The clcAE1/secYA1 and clcAE1/edgAE3 double mutants were less fit than the clcAE1 single mutant.
source: Similarly, when we constructed clcAE1/secYA1 and clcAE1/edgAE3 double mutants, we found that the double mutants were less fit than the clcAE1 single mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The seven mutations to secY cluster in a small region of the protein structure at the interface between the channel and plug.
source: In the crystal structure of the SecY homolog from Methanocaldococcus jannaschii (Van den Berg et al., 2004), these seven mutations cluster to the same region of the protein surface, at the interface of the channel pore and its blocking plug (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A and citation to Van den Berg et al., 2004

claim: Several of the secY mutations have been identified and characterized in the E. coli SecY homolog based on their ability to secrete proteins with mistranslated sequences.
source: Several of these mutations have been identified and characterized in the Escherichia coli SecY homolog (with 58% amino acid identity to M. extorquens DM4 SecY) based on their ability to secrete proteins with mistranslated sequences (Emr et al., 1981).
evidence: Supported by citation to Emr et al., 1981

claim: SecY mutations are predicted to disrupt interactions between the plug and pore, leading to a leaky channel.
source: These mutations are predicted to disrupt interactions between the plug and pore, leading to a leaky channel (Smith et al., 2005), and detailed biochemical investigation of one such mutant in E. coli demonstrated that this mutation allows the facilitated diffusion of small anions, most notably chloride (Dalal and Duong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2005 and Dalal and Duong, 2009

claim: A secY mutation in E. coli allows the facilitated diffusion of small anions, most notably chloride.
source: These mutations are predicted to disrupt interactions between the plug and pore, leading to a leaky channel (Smith et al., 2005), and detailed biochemical investigation of one such mutant in E. coli demonstrated that this mutation allows the facilitated diffusion of small anions, most notably chloride (Dalal and Duong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalal and Duong, 2009

claim: Mutations to the clcA promoter in isolates E1 and E2 lead to significantly increased transcription of clcA.
source: The two evolved PA1 isolates with clcA promoter mutations showed increased levels of clcA mRNA compared to either the ancestor or the PA1 isolate with a wild type clcA promoter (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The E. coli ClcA antiporter is capable of importing or exporting chloride, while necessarily transporting protons in the opposite direction.
source: However, the E. coli ClcA antiporter (with 33% amino acid identity to DM4) is capable of importing or exporting chloride, while necessarily transporting protons in the opposite direction (Accardi and Miller, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Accardi and Miller, 2004

claim: A transient decrease in intracellular pH upon addition of DCM was significantly larger in the strain overexpressing clcA.
source: We observed a transient decrease in intracellular pH upon addition of DCM that was significantly larger in the strain overexpressing clcA (Figure 4C), consistent with ClcA importing protons and exporting chloride.
evidence: Supported by pH biosensor data shown in Figure 4C

claim: ClcA imports protons and exports chloride during growth on DCM.
source: We observed a transient decrease in intracellular pH upon addition of DCM that was significantly larger in the strain overexpressing clcA (Figure 4C), consistent with ClcA importing protons and exporting chloride.
evidence: Inferred from pH biosensor data showing larger pH decrease with clcA overexpression

claim: The PA1 clcAE1 mutant was no more sensitive to NaCl or sucrose than the wild type strain.
source: In PA1, the clcAE1 mutant was no more sensitive to NaCl or sucrose than the wild type strain (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The PA1 secYA1 mutant was highly sensitive to NaCl, but only slightly more sensitive to sucrose.
source: In contrast, the PA1 secYA1 mutant was highly sensitive to NaCl, but only slightly more sensitive to sucrose (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 4D

claim: DM4 expressed significantly higher levels of clcA mRNA than the other three ancestral strains of M. extorquens tested.
source: However, we found that DM4 expressed significantly higher levels of clcA mRNA than the other three ancestral strains of M. extorquens tested (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The DM4 strain with the PA1 clcA promoter had decreased clcA expression and minimal growth with DCM as the sole carbon and energy source.
source: Consequently, we exchanged a 140-bp region upstream of clcA (containing a total of five nucleotide changes) between DM4 and PA1. The resulting DM4 strain with the PA1 clcA promoter had decreased clcA expression and minimal growth with DCM as the sole carbon and energy source, while the PA1 strain with the DM4 clcA promoter had increased clcA expression and was significantly more fit than the wild type PA1 strain (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The PA1 strain with the DM4 clcA promoter had increased clcA expression and was significantly more fit than the wild type PA1 strain.
source: Consequently, we exchanged a 140-bp region upstream of clcA (containing a total of five nucleotide changes) between DM4 and PA1. The resulting DM4 strain with the PA1 clcA promoter had decreased clcA expression and minimal growth with DCM as the sole carbon and energy source, while the PA1 strain with the DM4 clcA promoter had increased clcA expression and was significantly more fit than the wild type PA1 strain (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Complementing the DM4 clcAE0 mutant strain with a clcA/dcmA expression plasmid restored growth on DCM.
source: However, complementing the DM4 clcAE0 mutant strain with a clcA/dcmA expression plasmid restored growth on DCM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: The nucleotide sequences of secY, besA, and edgA in M. extorquens DM17 were exactly identical to M. extorquens AM1.
source: When we sequenced the secY, besA, and edgA loci in this strain, the nucleotide sequences were exactly identical to M. extorquens AM1.
evidence: Direct statement from sequencing results

claim: The clcA locus of DM17 contained an insertion sequence 52 bp upstream of the clcA promoter.
source: Compared to M. extorquens AM1, however, the clcA locus of DM17 contained an insertion sequence 52 bp upstream of the clcA promoter, and we found that clcA expression was even higher in DM17 than in DM4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by sequencing and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: clcA expression was even higher in DM17 than in DM4.
source: Compared to M. extorquens AM1, however, the clcA locus of DM17 contained an insertion sequence 52 bp upstream of the clcA promoter, and we found that clcA expression was even higher in DM17 than in DM4 (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Every strain showed higher fitness on DCM with the dual-expression dcmA/clcA plasmid than with the single-expression dcmA plasmid.
source: We found that every strain showed higher fitness on DCM with the dual-expression dcmA/clcA plasmid than with the single-expression dcmA plasmid (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by competitive fitness data shown in Figure 6

claim: Chloride export appears to be the most critical factor limiting growth on DCM in dcmA transconjugants.
source: By sequencing the evolved isolates, we identified mutations across diverse backgrounds that improve the ability to grow on DCM. Working backward from these mutations allowed us to determine that chloride accumulation appears to be the most critical factor limiting growth, and to identify multiple mechanisms that alleviate this stress.
evidence: Inferred from the repeated identification of mutations affecting chloride export genes

claim: Horizontal transfer of dcmA is not sufficient for efficient growth on DCM.
source: Horizontal transfer of dcmA is not sufficient for efficient growth on DCM and, in both the laboratory and the environment, microbes must also acquire refining mutations to optimize the newly-acquired pathway.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental evolution and analysis of natural isolates

claim: Microbes must acquire refining mutations to optimize the newly-acquired dcmA pathway in both the laboratory and the environment.
source: Horizontal transfer of dcmA is not sufficient for efficient growth on DCM and, in both the laboratory and the environment, microbes must also acquire refining mutations to optimize the newly-acquired pathway.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental evolution and analysis of natural isolates

claim: The observed mutations in secY are predicted to turn the protein translocase into a leaky chloride channel.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that chloride export was the key limiting factor during growth on DCM. First, the observed mutations in secY are predicted to turn the protein translocase into a leaky chloride channel, as demonstrated previously in E. coli (Dalal and Duong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dalal and Duong, 2009

claim: secY mutants are more sensitive to extracellular chloride.
source: Our growth rate measurements confirm that secY mutants are more sensitive to extracellular chloride, as we would expect if the mutant SecY facilitates chloride diffusion across the cell membrane.
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: Increased ClcA expression leads to increased proton import and chloride export.
source: The in vivo pH measurements upon DCM addition establish that ClcA imports protons, with a necessary concomitant export of chloride, and that increased ClcA expression leads to increased proton import and chloride export.
evidence: Supported by pH biosensor data shown in Figure 4C

claim: BesA is predicted to be a chloride channel.
source: Third, BesA is predicted to be a chloride channel (Sun et al., 2002) and while we cannot yet explain the mechanism by which the identified mutation would affect its function, we hypothesize that the mutation may also allow increased chloride export.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2002

claim: The besA mutation may allow increased chloride export.
source: Third, BesA is predicted to be a chloride channel (Sun et al., 2002) and while we cannot yet explain the mechanism by which the identified mutation would affect its function, we hypothesize that the mutation may also allow increased chloride export.
evidence: Hypothesis based on BesA being a chloride channel and the beneficial effect of the mutation

claim: All the mutations detected are addressing the same physiological limitation.
source: Finally, we observed that double mutants are no more fit than the best single mutant, suggesting that all the mutations we detected are addressing the same physiological limitation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of additivity in double mutant fitness

claim: EdgA is likely involved in chloride export.
source: Due to the antagonism of edgAE3 with clcAE1, it is likely that EdgA is also involved in chloride export.
evidence: Inferred from the antagonistic interaction between edgA and clcA mutations

claim: Using ClcA to export chloride, even at the cost of importing yet more protons, was highly beneficial.
source: There was no reason to expect that chloride was more toxic than protons, but using ClcA to export the chloride, even at the cost of importing yet more protons, was highly beneficial.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fitness data and pH measurements

claim: Excess intracellular chloride is either more toxic or less effectively managed than excess intracellular protons.
source: It appears that excess intracellular chloride is either more toxic or less effectively managed than excess intracellular protons.
evidence: Inferred from the benefit of chloride export despite proton import

claim: Mutations to human bestrophin homologs can lead to vitelliform macular dystrophy.
source: Mutations to human bestrophin homologs can lead to vitelliform macular dystrophy, but little is known about these proteins aside from their roles as chloride channels (Sun et al., 2002; Tsunenari et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2002 and Tsunenari et al., 2003

claim: Bacterial homologs of the bestrophin family are similarly uncharacterized.
source: Bacterial homologs of the bestrophin family are similarly uncharacterized.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge

claim: Select bacterial bestrophin homologs have been shown to affect swarming and sporulation.
source: Select bacterial homologs have been shown to affect swarming (Inoue et al., 2007) and sporulation (Rahn-Lee et al., 2009), but these systems have not explicitly replicated the role of the human homolog as a chloride channel.
evidence: Supported by citations to Inoue et al., 2007 and Rahn-Lee et al., 2009

claim: The Methylobacterium system may offer an opportunity to characterize the chloride transporter function of the bestrophin protein family in a tractable host with a strong linkage between BesA function and fitness.
source: However, our Methylobacterium system may offer an opportunity to characterize the chloride transporter function of this protein family in a tractable host with a strong linkage between BesA function and fitness.
evidence: Speculation about future research opportunities

claim: The analysis focused on mutations with very large fitness effects.
source: By design, our analysis has focused on mutations with very large fitness effects.
evidence: Direct statement about the study design

claim: Restricting the evolution experiment to 150 generations predominantly selected mutations that alleviate stresses imposed during growth on DCM.
source: Mutations that alleviate stresses imposed during growth on DCM had the potential to dramatically increase fitness, and restricting our evolution experiment to 150 generations predominantly selected these mutations.
evidence: Inference about the effect of experimental design

claim: The fitness effects of DCM-specific mutations appear to have been much larger than mutations that would be generally beneficial during growth in laboratory media.
source: Our populations undoubtedly sampled mutations that would be generally beneficial during growth in our media and laboratory conditions, as has been seen in earlier experiments with M. extorquens AM1 (Lee et al., 2009), but the fitness effects of these mutations appear to have been minor compared to the DCM-specific mutations.
evidence: Inference from the predominance of DCM-specific mutations and citation to Lee et al., 2009

claim: Isolate N1 lost an entire 458 kbp plasmid, which was likely due to selection but with a small fitness benefit as compared to acquiring a secY mutation.
source: For example, isolate N1 lost an entire 458 kbp plasmid, which was likely due to selection but with a small fitness benefit as compared to acquiring a secY mutation (Lee and Marx, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee and Marx, 2012

claim: Multiple lineages within a population independently arrived at solutions to increase chloride efflux.
source: We expect that multiple lineages within a population independently arrived at solutions to increase chloride efflux.
evidence: Inference from the observation of multiple different mutations affecting chloride export

claim: The size of the fitness effects produced evolutionary dynamics that resembled periodic selection.
source: However, the size of the fitness effects produced evolutionary dynamics that resembled periodic selection (Atwood et al., 1951), in which the first large effect mutation to arise in the population rapidly fixed.
evidence: Inference from evolutionary dynamics and citation to Atwood et al., 1951

claim: In population E2, the clcAE2 mutation fixed first, followed by the besAE2 mutation.
source: Population E2 is the exception, where the clcAE2 mutation fixed first, followed by the besAE2 mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by allele frequency data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: The inability to find improved isolates of M. radiotolerans stems from a combination of fewer accessible beneficial mutations, smaller fitness effects of the beneficial mutations, and a decreased sensitivity to the mutagenic effects of growing on DCM.
source: We hypothesize that our inability to find improved isolates of M. radiotolerans stems from a combination of fewer accessible beneficial mutations, smaller fitness effects of the beneficial mutations, and a decreased sensitivity to the mutagenic effects of growing on DCM (Perez-Pantoja et al., 2013).
evidence: Hypothesis to explain lack of evolution in M. radiotolerans, with citation to Perez-Pantoja et al., 2013

claim: There are few examples where mutations that arise during laboratory evolution can also be identified in natural populations.
source: Experimental evolution is increasingly used to simulate natural evolutionary processes (Kawecki et al., 2012); however, there are few examples where mutations that arise during laboratory evolution can also be identified in natural populations (Wong et al., 2012; Traverse et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kawecki et al., 2012, Wong et al., 2012, and Traverse et al., 2013

claim: Parallel mutations to clcA have arisen in two independent DCM-degrading environmental isolates of M. extorquens.
source: We have shown that mutations to clcA can be highly beneficial during laboratory growth, and that parallel mutations to clcA have arisen in two independent DCM-degrading environmental isolates of M. extorquens.
evidence: Supported by sequencing and expression data for DM4 and DM17

claim: In M. extorquens DM4, nucleotide mutations in the clcA promoter can be directly linked to clcA overexpression and increased organismal fitness during growth on DCM.
source: In the reference environmental isolate M. extorquens DM4, we can directly link nucleotide mutations in the clcA promoter to clcA overexpression and increased organismal fitness during growth on DCM.
evidence: Supported by promoter swap experiments shown in Figure 5B

claim: Transconjugants that received both the catabolic gene dcmA and the chloride exporter gene clcA were more efficient at degrading DCM than those that received dcmA alone.
source: In our example of DCM degradation, transconjugants that received both the catabolic gene dcmA and the chloride exporter gene clcA were more efficient at degrading DCM than those that received dcmA alone (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by competitive fitness data shown in Figure 6

claim: Post-transfer refinement of microbial hosts is widespread in nature.
source: Based on recent examples from metabolic engineering, we expect that these types of host–pathway interactions are common (Kizer et al., 2008; Ro et al., 2008; Verwaal et al., 2010; Michener et al., 2012; Bernhardt and Urlacher, 2014) and, consequently, that post–transfer refinement of microbial hosts is also widespread in nature.
evidence: Inference based on citations to metabolic engineering examples

claim: The approach of deliberate horizontal transfer in the laboratory followed by experimental evolution offers an opportunity to identify both the limiting stresses and the mutations that can overcome these stresses.
source: Our approach of deliberate horizontal transfer in the laboratory followed by experimental evolution offers an opportunity to identify both the limiting stresses and the mutations that can overcome these stresses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the results of this study

claim: Microbes frequently acquire genetic material from organisms that are distant evolutionary relatives but close ecological neighbors.
source: Microbes frequently acquire genetic material from organisms that are distant evolutionary relatives but close ecological neighbors (Ochman et al., 2000; Gogarten et al., 2002; Smillie et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ochman et al., 2000, Gogarten et al., 2002, and Smillie et al., 2011

claim: Horizontally-transferred genes and pathways play important roles in processes ranging from the spread of antibiotic resistance to ecological differentiation.
source: These horizontally-transferred genes and pathways play important roles in processes ranging from the spread of antibiotic resistance to ecological differentiation (Forsberg et al., 2012; Shapiro et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forsberg et al., 2012 and Shapiro et al., 2012

claim: Horizontal gene transfer can speed the assembly and dissemination of a catabolic pathway when a new environmental niche opens up through the introduction of a xenobiotic compound.
source: When, for example, a new environmental niche opens up through the introduction of a xenobiotic compound, horizontal gene transfer (HGT) can speed the assembly and dissemination of a corresponding catabolic pathway (Springael and Top, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Springael and Top, 2004

claim: Newly-acquired abilities may be costly for the host until they are carefully integrated into existing metabolic and regulatory networks.
source: However, newly-acquired abilities may be costly for the host until they are carefully integrated into existing metabolic and regulatory networks (Kim and Copley, 2012; Yadid et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim and Copley, 2012 and Yadid et al., 2013

claim: Productively transferring genes and pathways into new hosts often requires significant post-transfer refinement in metabolic engineering.
source: The challenges associated with such adaptations are highlighted by many examples from metabolic engineering, where productively transferring genes and pathways into new hosts often requires significant post–transfer refinement (Chang et al., 2007; Michener et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang et al., 2007 and Michener et al., 2012
